content: The FDA is expected to review and potentially approve cabotegravir injections for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) within 2-3 months following the publication of this guideline. All materials in this publication are in the public domain and may be used or reprinted without permission, though citation of the source is appreciated. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is not responsible for the content of external websites, and the URLs listed were current as of the publication date. In anticipation of the likely FDA approval of cabotegravir (CAB) for PrEP in late 2021, a new section has been added to the guidelines. This section addresses prescribing PrEP with intramuscular CAB injections every two months for sexually active men, women, and transgender individuals who meet the indications for PrEP use. The guidelines now include a recommendation to inform all sexually active adults and adolescents about PrEP (graded as IIIB). Additionally, conditional on FDA approval, PrEP with intramuscular CAB injections is recommended for HIV prevention in adults reporting sexual behaviors that place them at substantial ongoing risk of HIV exposure and acquisition (graded as IA). Specific clinical guidance for CAB has been added, recognizing that CAB has a different dosing and follow-up schedule compared to oral PrEP. Unlike oral PrEP, CAB does not require renal or lipid monitoring. The determination of indications for PrEP use in sexually active individuals has been simplified. Flow charts have replaced boxes to assess indications for both sexually active individuals and persons who inject drugs. The HIV testing algorithm has been revised to include two separate algorithms: one for assessing HIV status in individuals with no recent antiretroviral exposure who are starting or restarting PrEP, and another for assessing HIV status during follow-up visits for individuals currently or recently taking PrEP. F/TAF (emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) has been added as an FDA-approved option for sexually active men and transgender women at risk of HIV acquisition. However, the FDA approval for F/TAF excludes individuals at risk through receptive vaginal sex, including cisgender women. The sections on initiation and follow-up care have been revised and reordered. Guidelines applicable to all PrEP patients are described first, followed by those specific to selected patients. The frequency of assessing estimated creatinine clearance (eCrCl) has been revised to every 12 months for individuals under 50 years of age or with eCrCl ≥90 mL/min at PrEP initiation, and every 6 months for all other patients. Medications have been added to the list of drug interactions for TAF. Options for PrEP initiation and follow-up care via telehealth (Tele-PrEP) have been outlined. Procedures for providing or prescribing PrEP medications on the same day as the initial evaluation (same-day PrEP) have also been included. Additionally, procedures for off-label prescription of TDF/FTC (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine) to men who have sex with men (MSM) on a non-daily regimen (2-1-1) and their follow-up care have been outlined. A brief section on primary care considerations for PrEP patients has been added, along with a section on providing CAB for PrEP. Evidence reviews for CAB trials have been updated and moved to an appendix. Clinical trial results for transgender women and MSM have been separated into distinct rows in evidence tables. For more clinical advice about PrEP guidelines, clinicians can contact the National Clinicians Consultation Center PrEPline or visit the CDC HIV website for resources. The guidelines emphasize that daily oral PrEP with emtricitabine (F) combined with either tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) has been shown to be safe and effective in reducing the risk of sexual HIV acquisition. All sexually active adults and adolescents should be informed about PrEP. Daily F/TDF is recommended for HIV prevention in sexually active adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg who report behaviors placing them at substantial ongoing risk of HIV exposure and acquisition. Daily F/TAF is recommended for sexually active men and transgender women at risk of HIV acquisition but is not recommended for women or individuals at risk through receptive vaginal sex due to a lack of efficacy and safety data in these populations. Renal function should be assessed at baseline for PrEP patients taking daily oral F/TDF or F/TAF and monitored periodically. For patients over 50 years of age or with eCrCl <90 mL/min at initiation, renal function should be assessed every 6 months. For all other daily oral PrEP patients, eCrCl should be assessed at least every 12 months. Conditional on FDA approval, PrEP with intramuscular CAB injections is recommended for HIV prevention in adults and adolescents reporting sexual behaviors that place them at substantial ongoing risk of HIV exposure and acquisition. Acute and chronic HIV infection must be excluded by symptom history and HIV testing immediately before prescribing any PrEP regimen. HIV infection should be assessed at least every 3 months for patients taking daily oral PrEP and every 2 months for those receiving CAB injections to prevent the continuation of PrEP in individuals with incident HIV infection. The guidelines also highlight the importance of providing access to medication adherence support and additional proven risk-reduction services to enhance the effectiveness of PrEP. These services may include behavioral risk reduction counseling, access to clean needles/syringes, and drug treatment services for persons who inject drugs. The guidelines recommend gender-inclusive models of PrEP care to address the needs of all individuals who could benefit from its use, including cisgender and transgender adults and adolescents, as well as persons who inject drugs. The intended users of these guidelines include primary care clinicians, infectious disease specialists, and other healthcare providers involved in HIV prevention and care. The guidelines underscore the need for equitable provision of PrEP to populations at the highest risk of HIV acquisition, as disparities in PrEP use persist among African Americans, Hispanics, women, and residents of southern states. These populations are disproportionately affected by HIV but have lower rates of PrEP use compared to their risk levels. Finally, the guidelines emphasize the importance of routine sexual history-taking as a necessary step to identify patients at risk of HIV acquisition and to provide appropriate sexual health care. Clinicians should ensure confidentiality and create a supportive environment to encourage open discussions about sexual and substance use behaviors.
